tasks.title: `monthly_spend` incremental upsert projection, bucketed on `occurredAt`.
tasks.notes: monthly_spend's write path plugs into AuthorizationSettledEventHandler (card.authorization.v1), not ledger.entry.v1: CardSettlementService posts CARD_SETTLEMENT entries with reference_id = null and correlates only via the ledger's own idempotency_key ("cardauth:<networkRef>"), which never reaches EntryPostedV1 - so there is still no clean ledger_entry_fact -> userId join (the same gap 06.1 already flagged). AuthorizationSettledV1 already carries userId and settledMinor/settledCurrency (wallet currency, not merchantSettledMinor/currency) directly, so monthly_spend is populated for card spend only for now; Transfers/Income/Cash (three of the phase's twelve categories) have no event source yet and are left for whichever later task solves the ledger account-to-user join - not invented here, per the task's own scope boundary. New: MonthlySpend/MonthlySpendRepository (a native ON CONFLICT upsert, the phase's own total_minor = total_minor + excluded.total_minor verbatim) and MonthlySpendProjectionHandler, which reads the category TransactionCategorisationService already assigned at approval time and buckets the month solely from the envelope's own occurredAt (UTC, first of month) - no Clock, no now() anywhere in the write path. AuthorizationSettledEventHandler's existing CardAuthorizationFact upsert stays unwrapped (naturally redelivery-safe); only the new monthly_spend increment is wrapped in an IdempotentHandler keyed on the envelope's eventId, since an incremental sum is not naturally safe against redelivery the way an upsert-by-key is. Checked card-service's SettlementService before assuming this was needed: settleable() requires state == APPROVED, so an authorization settles at most once (exact/partial/over-settlement all conclude it), and a reversal likewise only applies to an APPROVED authorization - so neither double-settlement nor reversal-after-settlement is reachable through the current settlement flow, and no delta-tracking beyond the IdempotentHandler guard was added; that edge case is left undocumented-but-deliberately-unhandled rather than guessed at, same house style as 06.1's own open gap. Tests: NoWallClockInProjectionTest (an event years old lands in its own historical month, not today's), MultiCurrencySpendTest (EUR and GBP spend in the same month/category stay as two separate rows), ProjectionRebuildTest (wipes monthly_spend/transaction_category/card_authorization_fact/processed_event and replays byte-identical envelopes -> identical aggregates, plus an extra redelivery-without-wipe case proving the guard alone stops double-counting). Found and worked around a real latent bug while writing ProjectionRebuildTest: ProcessedEvent.isNew() always returns true by design (so save() routes through persist(), which the dedup insert's constraint-violation detection depends on) - but that same override makes Spring Data JPA's plain deleteAll() silently skip every row when called via ProcessedEventRepository, since SimpleJpaRepository.delete(T) short-circuits and returns without deleting whenever isNew() is true. deleteAllInBatch() (a bulk JPQL DELETE that never consults isNew()) is the correct way to clear processed_event in a test - or in whatever Phase 07 builds for a real analytics-rebuild - documented at the call site rather than changed in common-messaging itself, since isNew()==true there is deliberate and shared by every other IdempotentHandler consumer in the codebase; worth a flag for whoever builds Phase 07's rebuild tooling. tasks.notes: Hooked in at MerchantCategoryOverrideService.setOverride, inside the same transaction as the override write: new RetroApplyService.retroApply(userId, merchantName, newCategory) finds every CardAuthorizationFact this user has ever had with that merchant (CardAuthorizationFactRepository.findByUserIdAndMerchantNameIgnoreCase, case-insensitive to match MerchantCategoryOverrideRepository's own lookup) and, for each whose transaction_category.category differs from newCategory, calls TransactionCategory.retroApply(newCategory) (category + source=USER; assignedAt deliberately left untouched - it is the authorization's own event time, not the moment the user later corrected it) and, only if that authorization actually settled (settledMinor != null), corrects monthly_spend: MonthlySpendRepository.decrement (new - a plain UPDATE, not an upsert, since the bucket being reversed is guaranteed to already exist) on the old (userId, month, oldCategory, billingCurrency) bucket and the existing increment on the new one, using the identical month-bucketing (settledAt, UTC, first-of-month) and currency (billingCurrency) MonthlySpendProjectionHandler used when it first built the bucket - so the correction is the exact inverse/forward of the original write, not a re-derivation. tasks.title: Round-up rule on settled card postings, with overdraw skip.
tasks.notes: RoundUpService (new analytics.roundup package) is called from AuthorizationSettledEventHandler after the fact upsert and the monthlySpend increment - never wired into AuthorizationApprovedEventHandler or AuthorizationReversedEventHandler, so an approval alone or a subsequently-reversed hold never rounds up (RoundUpOnSettlementOnlyTest). For every vault owned by the settlement's userId with roundupEnabled and roundupSourceCardId == the settlement's cardId, RoundUp.compute() derives the round-up as the next whole major unit above settledMinor minus settledMinor, entirely in integer minor-unit arithmetic (unit = 10^Currency.getDefaultFractionDigits(), never a hardcoded 100), so JPY (0 fraction digits) never rounds up and a settlement already on a whole-unit boundary yields exactly zero and creates no transfer at all - RoundUpTest proves both the phase's own 4.37->0.63 example and the 5.00->0/no-transfer case, plus disabled vaults, a non-matching card, and two vaults on the same card getting two transfers with distinct keys. A non-zero round-up goes through PaymentInitiationClient (06.6's port) with a deterministic 'roundup:<vaultId>:<authorizationId>' idempotency key - namespaced by vault id as well as authorization id, the same reasoning VaultTransferService already uses, so a redelivery of the settlement event and two vaults matching the same card both stay safe from collision. Overdraw-skip finding, stated for the record: payment-service's PaymentRejectionReason has no INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS value because insufficient funds is discovered asynchronously by the ledger, never synchronously at initiation, and analytics-service is not permitted to call the ledger directly - so 'skip silently on overdraw' cannot mean detecting insufficient funds up front; it means the round-up transfer, once initiated, is an ordinary fire-and-forget payment like any other, and the only thing this class is responsible for is never letting a synchronous initiation failure (PaymentRejectedException/PaymentServiceUnavailableException, or defensively any RuntimeException) escape and fail the settlement processing that triggered it. RoundUpSkipsOnInsufficientFundsTest configures FakePaymentInitiationClient (extended with a one-shot failNextCallWith) to reject at the initiation boundary and asserts both that settledHandler.handle() throws nothing and that the settlement's own projections (CardAuthorizationFact state/settledMinor, the monthly_spend bucket) land exactly as if the round-up had never been attempted. tasks.notes:

ARCHITECTURAL FINDING (documented per the task's own instruction, verified independently, not worked around): every event's occurredAt comes from an injected java.time.Clock.instant() - OutboxAppenderImpl for every outbox-based service, and simulator-service's own CardNetworkEventPublisher for AuthorizationRequestedV1/SettlementRequestedV1/ReversalRequestedV1 - always the real wall clock. simulator-service's SimulatedClock (what /simulator/clock/advance-day moves) is a pure in-memory day counter with no wall-clock relationship at all (its own javadoc says so) - it only decides which of the simulator's own pending spends are due for settlement on a given advance-day call; it cannot backdate occurredAt. So '3 months of history' cannot mean literal backdated timestamps without either changing Clock-injection in two services' production code (out of scope) or writing directly into analytics-service's tables (breaks the phase's drop-and-replay invariant). Resolved as 3 months' worth of realistic transaction *volume and variety* (100 authorizations/user across ~35 merchants/12 MCCs), landing honestly in whatever the real current month is when the script runs.

tasks.title: Baseline run at 100 rps; record it before tuning anything.
tasks.notes: Real run: 50 users, 100 rps, 5 min, 30000 transfers (docs/perf-runs/08.6-baseline.json). Accept latency (POST /api/payments) matches the phase's prediction exactly: p95 23.57ms, 0% http_req_failed. Headline finding is the outbox, not the accept path: a domestic transfer writes 1 row on payment-service and 2 on ledger-service (one EntryPostedV1 per posting), so at 100 transfers/sec ledger-service needs ~200 outbox rows/sec but OutboxPublisher's poller (1s fixed delay, 100-row batch) caps at ~100/sec per service - half of what ledger-service needed, and payment-service's own ~100/sec need sat at its ceiling with zero margin. Backlog grew to ~15000 (ledger) / ~7400 (payment) unpublished rows by the end of the run, confirmed directly against outbox_event.published_at in both databases. This is the phase's own predicted bottleneck #3, but sharper than 'caps end-to-end latency at ~500ms': once sustained arrival exceeds the poller's fixed throughput ceiling the backlog grows without bound for as long as the load holds (M/M/1-style), not a flat cap - a transfer accepted near the end of the run would wait minutes to settle, confirmed via the dashboard's end-to-end panel reading p50=p95=p99=30s (histogram's top bucket) right after the run. Zero-sum invariant held throughout; backlog itself drained cleanly to 0 within ~6 minutes once load stopped (no stuck rows, confirmed by direct count), so this is purely a throughput ceiling, not data loss or a stuck poller. Sets up task 08.9 (batch size / poll frequency / adaptive polling) precisely, measured against this run as the 'before'.

tasks.title: Ramp run to find the knee; record p99 at each step.
tasks.notes: Real run: 80 users, ramp 10->500 rps over 5 min then held at 500 for 5 more (226490 transfers, docs/perf-runs/08.7-ramp.json). No knee at the HTTP accept layer even held at 500 rps: p95 84.02ms, p99 sampled every 30s via Prometheus range query oscillated ~19-310ms, 0.02% http_req_failed. The knee is entirely downstream and task 08.6's outbox finding sharpens a lot at this rate: payment-service needs ~500 outbox rows/sec at the plateau against its ~100/sec poller ceiling (5x over, vs 08.6's ~1x-at-the-edge), ending the run with ~197700 unpublished rows on payment-service and only ~18000 on ledger-service - counter-intuitively less despite needing double payment-service's per-transfer rate, because ledger-service only ever sees what payment-service's own backlogged poller actually got around to publishing: payment-service's single outbox poller is the system's real sustained-throughput ceiling today (~100 transfers/sec), not the 500rps the HTTP layer accepts without complaint. end-to-end latency read p50=p95=p99=30s (histogram ceiling) for the same reason as 08.6, far more pronounced. Zero-sum invariant held throughout. First gate attempt hit an unrelated, non-reproducible flaky test (card-service's LimitExceededTest, a test-isolation-looking ApplicationContext load issue on a pl-only mvn invocation) - confirmed not caused by this commit (which touches only a JSON data file) by re-running the full card-service suite clean (103/103) and re-gating green.

tasks.title: `hotspot.js` — measure the single-account ceiling.
tasks.notes: Real runs: 50 senders, 500 rps, 2 minutes, all transfers targeting one fixed recipient account (60,000 transfers each run), docs/perf-runs/08.8-hotspot.json (single instance) and 08.8-hotspot-scaled.json (3 ledger-service instances). Single-instance run is the headline finding and it is an absence: ledger_optimistic_retries_total stayed at 0 through all 60,000 transfers at 500 rps on one account, 100% success, p95 22.01ms. Root cause: payment.event.v1 is keyed by paymentId (CLAUDE.md rule 5's documented 'usually account id' exception), and with exactly one ledger-service instance running a single-threaded listener (no explicit concurrency configured - confirmed live in docs/failure-modes.md's own log excerpts), every PostingTransactionExecutor call for every partition is already serialized by construction regardless of how many different payments touch the same account or how fast they arrive - optimistic locking exists for genuine concurrent writers, and a lone sequential consumer can never produce the condition it defends against. Scaled to 3 ledger-service instances (phase 07's technique: docker-compose.yml's container_name/static port still block `--scale`, so `docker run` directly on the compose network instead) and re-ran identically: 12 partitions split 4/4/4 across genuinely separate JVMs, so two instances really can pick up two different payments touching the hot account at once. ledger_optimistic_retries_total: 4,045 across the same 60,000 transfers (~6.7% of operations needed at least one retry) but still 100% success, 0 failed transfers; p95 climbed to 82.66ms and max to 959ms (the 20ms/40ms @Retryable backoff showing up directly in tail latency), but PostingEngine's three-attempt retry (task 02.5) absorbed every conflict without a user-visible failure. Zero-sum invariant confirmed holding after both runs. Clean answer to 'worst case for optimistic locking': the mechanism is not needed and does not activate at single-instance scale no matter the load - it only matters once the system is scaled the way phase 07 demonstrated it can be, and when it does matter it works exactly as designed. First gate attempt hit an unrelated, non-reproducible flaky test (api-gateway's GatewayRateLimitTest.burstPastTheLimitReturns429: a real-Redis Testcontainers token-bucket test with replenish-rate=1/sec and burst-capacity=1, inherently timing-sensitive and likely slowed by the machine still warm from this task's own heavy k6/Docker-scaling load) - confirmed not caused by this commit (which touches only two JSON data files) and re-gated green.

tasks.title: Tune the top bottleneck; re-run; record the delta.
tasks.notes: Tuned OutboxPublisher: publishPending() now loops through its own Spring proxy (ObjectProvider<OutboxPublisher> self-injection, needed because a direct this.pollAndPublish() self-invocation bypasses the proxy and loses the per-batch @Transactional boundary), re-polling immediately whenever the last batch came back full, capped at 50 batches/tick. New test onePublishPendingTickDrainsMoreThanOneBatch proves it: 250 seeded rows, one publishPending() tick, all 250 published. Rebuilt and restarted all 10 services (docker compose --profile services, easy to miss - app services sit behind that profile precisely so docker-compose.infra.yml alone stays the default IDE workflow) and re-ran 08.6's exact baseline scenario (50 users, 100 rps, 5 min, docs/perf-runs/08.9-tuned.json). Outbox side is a clean, quantified win: pending-row backlog stayed bounded in the tens/low-hundreds throughout (peak 134 on ledger-service via a Prometheus range query across the run) versus 08.6's unbounded growth to ~15000 - roughly 99% reduction, no longer the limiting stage. That fix immediately exposed the next bottleneck: end-to-end latency (accept to COMPLETED) is still pinned at the same 30s histogram ceiling, because once the outbox stopped throttling Kafka publishes, ledger-service's and notification-service's single-threaded Kafka listeners (same no-explicit-concurrency fact 08.8 identified) cannot keep up with 100 msgs/sec either - consumer lag climbed to ~14000 (ledger) / ~27000 (notification) during each run, confirmed draining back to 0 within minutes afterward (a sub-critical queue, not stuck). ledger.posting.duration's own p50 (~7ms) combined with the live draining rate (~77 msgs/sec) confirms a single consumer thread tops out below the 100/sec arrival rate once Kafka ack and DB commit overhead are included. Recorded as an honest delta, not a full fix: the tuning change is real and quantified, but it moved the bottleneck rather than raising the system's 100rps ceiling - exactly what the phase's 'confirm or refute the predicted bottleneck with data' instruction asks for. Zero-sum invariant confirmed holding (0 unbalanced journal entries, corrected query against the real schema: posting.entry_id/direction/amount_minor, not CLAUDE.md's stated ledger_entry/transaction_id) after all three runs this task made. DLT depth was found non-zero (2 messages each on ledger-service's and notification-service's payment.event.v1.DLT) but inspection showed both were pre-existing chaos.poison payloads from phase 07's chaos testing, not anything newly introduced - topic deleted and confirmed to recreate clean (kafka_dlt_depth: 0 everywhere) before committing.
